--- title: Categorical Predictors author: - name: Benjamin Vincent description: "Model string and categorical columns with treatment coding, choose the reference level, shrink many levels with a hierarchical prior, and intervene by label with do()." tags: - Causal Inference - do-Operator - Hierarchical Effects - Categorical Predictors - Priors - Simulation image: thumbnails/categorical_predictors.png jupyter: pathmc bread-crumbs: false --- Many causal questions are about *which group* a unit belongs to rather than *how much* of something it received: which sales region a store sits in, which message variant a customer saw, which policy regime a country adopted. These predictors arrive as strings or pandas categoricals, and a regression cannot multiply a coefficient by `"north"`. The usual workaround is to build indicator columns by hand: ```python dummies = pd.get_dummies(df["region"], drop_first=True) # region_south, region_west ``` That works until it doesn't: the reference level is whichever value happens to sort first, new data with a missing or extra level silently produces a different set of columns, and an intervention such as "move every store to the south region" has to be translated by hand into flipping two indicator columns. pathmc handles categorical predictors as a first-class part of the DSL instead. When you build a model, it detects string and categorical columns, expands each one into indicator columns using **treatment coding**, gives every non-reference level its own named coefficient, and — the part that matters for causal work — **freezes the level set and reference** so that `predict()` and `do()` can never silently recompute the coding on new data. Interventions then read the way you would say them: `model.do(set={"region": "south"})`. This notebook walks through the full surface: automatic inference, explicit `C()` syntax, the two coding schemes, priors (including hierarchical shrinkage), interventions by label, prediction on new rows, and the boundaries of what is supported today. ::: {.callout-note} ## Prerequisites This example assumes you are comfortable with the pathmc DSL (see [Model Specification](/user-guide/model-specification.html)) and with the idea of an intervention as graph surgery (see [The do() Operator](causal_do_operator.qmd)). Everything else is introduced as we go. ::: ## Setup and simulated data We simulate a store-level dataset with three sales regions and one continuous covariate. The data-generating process is deliberately simple so every estimate can be checked against a planted truth: $$ y_i = 1 + 0.5\,x_i + \delta_{\text{region}_i} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5^2) $$ with region effects $\delta_{\text{north}} = 0$, $\delta_{\text{south}} = 2$, and $\delta_{\text{west}} = -1$. Group sizes are unequal on purpose — 150 north, 100 south, 50 west — because unbalanced groups are the norm in observational data and they matter later when we discuss priors. ::: {#aa985525 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import arviz as az import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde import pathmc from pathmc import Prior FIG_WIDTH = 7 FIG_HEIGHT = 4 COLORS = {"north": "#1f77b4", "south": "#ff7f0e", "west": "#2ca02c"} LEVELS = ["north", "south", "west"] TRUE_INTERCEPT = 1.0 TRUE_SLOPE_X = 0.5 TRUE_EFFECT = {"north": 0.0, "south": 2.0, "west": -1.0} TRUE_GROUP_MEAN = {k: TRUE_INTERCEPT + v for k, v in TRUE_EFFECT.items()} rng = np.random.default_rng(11) region = np.repeat(LEVELS, [150, 100, 50]) rng.shuffle(region) x = rng.normal(size=region.size) y = ( TRUE_INTERCEPT + TRUE_SLOPE_X * x + np.array([TRUE_EFFECT[r] for r in region]) + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=region.size) ) df = pd.DataFrame({"y": y, "x": x, "region": region}) df.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
y x region
0 -0.614373 -0.941384 west
1 1.339371 0.791763 north
2 0.983779 -0.505302 north
3 0.437651 -1.090653 north
4 3.579574 0.365249 south
``` ::: ::: The causal structure is the simplest possible: both `region` and `x` are exogenous causes of `y`, with no confounding between them (@fig-categorical-dag). ```{dot} //| label: fig-categorical-dag //| fig-cap: "Causal graph for the simulated data. Both the categorical predictor region and the continuous covariate x are exogenous parents of the outcome y." //| fig-width: 4 digraph { rankdir=LR node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded"] region [label="region\n{north, south, west}", fillcolor="#c6dbef"] x [label="x", fillcolor="#c6dbef"] y [label="y", fillcolor="#fcbba1"] region -> y x -> y } ``` @fig-outcome-by-region shows the raw outcome by region. The group means sit close to the planted values of 1, 3, and 0, and the smaller west group is visibly noisier. ::: {#cell-fig-outcome-by-region .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIG_WIDTH, FIG_HEIGHT)) for i, level in enumerate(LEVELS): mask = df["region"] == level jitter = rng.uniform(-0.25, 0.25, size=mask.sum()) ax.scatter(i + jitter, df.loc[mask, "y"], s=12, alpha=0.5, color=COLORS[level]) ax.hlines( TRUE_GROUP_MEAN[level], i - 0.35, i + 0.35, colors=COLORS[level], linestyles="--", linewidth=2, ) ax.set_xticks(range(len(LEVELS))) ax.set_xticklabels([f"{lvl}\n(n = {(df['region'] == lvl).sum()})" for lvl in LEVELS]) ax.set_xlabel("Region") ax.set_ylabel("Outcome y") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Observed outcome y by region (jittered points) with the true group mean at x = 0 as a dashed line in each region's color. Group sizes are 150 (north), 100 (south), and 50 (west).](categorical_predictors_files/figure-html/fig-outcome-by-region-output-1.png){#fig-outcome-by-region width=663 height=374} ::: ::: ## Treatment coding, in pictures A regression cannot multiply a coefficient by the word "south". The standard fix is **treatment coding** (also called dummy or reference coding). One level is chosen as the **reference** and absorbed into the intercept; every other level receives an indicator column that is 1 for rows in that level and 0 otherwise. For our three regions with `north` as reference, the linear predictor becomes $$ \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_x\,x_i + \beta_{\text{south}}\,\mathbb{1}[\text{region}_i = \text{south}] + \beta_{\text{west}}\,\mathbb{1}[\text{region}_i = \text{west}] $$ so that $\beta_0$ is the expected outcome for a north store at $x = 0$, and $\beta_{\text{south}}$ and $\beta_{\text{west}}$ are the **differences** from north. Each row of the data therefore maps to one of three indicator patterns: | `region` | `region[T.south]` | `region[T.west]` | Expected outcome at $x = 0$ | |---|---|---|---| | north (reference) | 0 | 0 | $\beta_0$ | | south | 1 | 0 | $\beta_0 + \beta_{\text{south}}$ | | west | 0 | 1 | $\beta_0 + \beta_{\text{west}}$ | @fig-treatment-coding shows this for the first rows of our data. The `T.` in the column names is the conventional marker for a treatment contrast against the reference. ::: {#cell-fig-treatment-coding .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} preview = pathmc.model("y ~ x + region", data=df).design("y") indicator_cols = [c for c in preview.columns if c.startswith("region[")] block = preview[indicator_cols].head(12).to_numpy() labels = df["region"].head(12).tolist() from matplotlib.colors import to_rgb column_levels = [c[len("region[T.") : -1] for c in indicator_cols] rgb = np.ones(block.shape + (3,)) for c, level in enumerate(column_levels): rgb[block[:, c] == 1, c, :] = to_rgb(COLORS[level]) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIG_WIDTH, FIG_HEIGHT * 1.1)) ax.imshow(rgb, aspect="auto") for r in range(block.shape[0]): for c in range(block.shape[1]): ax.text( c, r, int(block[r, c]), ha="center", va="center", color="white" if block[r, c] else "black", fontsize=10, ) ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, len(indicator_cols)), minor=True) ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, len(labels)), minor=True) ax.grid(which="minor", color="lightgray", linewidth=0.8) ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0) ax.set_xticks(range(len(indicator_cols))) ax.set_xticklabels(indicator_cols) ax.set_yticks(range(len(labels))) ax.set_yticklabels(labels) for tick, label in zip(ax.get_yticklabels(), labels): tick.set_color(COLORS[label]) ax.set_xlabel("Design-matrix column") ax.set_ylabel("Row's region value") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Treatment-coded indicator block for the first twelve rows. Each row's region label (left) selects at most one indicator column; north rows are all zeros because north is the reference level absorbed by the intercept.](categorical_predictors_files/figure-html/fig-treatment-coding-output-1.png){#fig-treatment-coding width=664 height=412} ::: ::: ## Automatic inference from the data The simplest specification lists the column like any other predictor. pathmc inspects the data at build time and treats the column as categorical because it holds strings. ::: {#5eeb6936 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} model = pathmc.model("y ~ x + region", data=df) model.equations() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=4} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{y,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\[6pt] \mu_{y} &= \beta_{0,\,y} + \mathrm{x} + \operatorname{C}(\mathrm{region};\,\mathrm{ref}=north;\,\mathrm{levels}=\{north, south, west\}) \\ \mathrm{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{y},\, \sigma_{y}) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: The equation display is a term-level shorthand: `x` stands for the slope term $\beta_x x_i$, and `C(region; ...)` stands for the whole block of level indicators and their coefficients. What it records is everything the compiler froze about the categorical: the variable, the reference level, and the full ordered level set. The design matrix confirms the indicator columns sit alongside the continuous predictor: ::: {#a813f747 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.design("y").head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
Intercept x region[T.south] region[T.west]
0 1.0 -0.941384 0.0 1.0
1 1.0 0.791763 0.0 0.0
2 1.0 -0.505302 0.0 0.0
3 1.0 -1.090653 0.0 0.0
4 1.0 0.365249 1.0 0.0
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Which columns count as categorical? pathmc infers a plain term as categorical when the column is any of: - a **pandas `Categorical`** dtype (declared category order is respected — see below), - a **pandas `StringDtype`** column, - an **`object`** column whose non-missing values are strings or bytes. An `object` column that merely *holds* numbers (for example, integers stored as Python objects) stays continuous. Integer and float columns are always continuous unless you wrap them in `C()`. Polars and other narwhals-compatible frames are converted to pandas for this inspection, so the same rules apply. ::: ### Parameter names and coordinates Categorical coefficients live in their own vector, separate from the equation's flat `beta_y` vector that holds the intercept and continuous slopes. The name is always `beta_{outcome}_{variable}`, and the vector carries an xarray coordinate `{outcome}_{variable}_levels` whose labels are the represented levels: ::: {#50773824 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.priors() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=6} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{y,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: ::: {#cf107396 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} {name: list(values) for name, values in model.pymc_model.coords.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` {'y_predictors': ['Intercept', 'x'], 'y_region_levels': ['south', 'west']} ``` ::: ::: Because `beta_y_region` is indexed by level name rather than position, posteriors read naturally in `summary()` and ArviZ without ever reconstructing patsy's column order. ## Fit and check against the truth ::: {#77283d65 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} idata = model.fit(random_seed=42, progressbar=False) az.summary( idata, var_names=["beta_y", "beta_y_region", "sigma_y"], ci_prob=0.94, ci_kind="hdi", round_to=2, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` NUTS[nutpie]: [beta_y_region, beta_y, sigma_y] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
mean sd hdi94_lb hdi94_ub ess_bulk ess_tail r_hat mcse_mean mcse_sd
beta_y[Intercept] 1.01 0.04 0.93 1.09 2149.09 2506.59 1.0 0.0 0.0
beta_y[x] 0.51 0.03 0.45 0.57 4359.37 3189.37 1.0 0.0 0.0
beta_y_region[south] 1.96 0.07 1.83 2.09 2242.07 2683.62 1.0 0.0 0.0
beta_y_region[west] -1.07 0.09 -1.23 -0.90 2728.12 2704.13 1.0 0.0 0.0
sigma_y 0.53 0.02 0.49 0.57 4305.59 3168.37 1.0 0.0 0.0
``` ::: ::: Before going further we verify that the workflow recovers the planted values. @fig-level-effects-recovery puts the posterior for each region contrast next to its truth: $\beta_{\text{south}} = 2$ and $\beta_{\text{west}} = -1$. ::: {#cell-fig-level-effects-recovery .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} def forest_by_level(ax, post, coord, truth, colors, offset=0.0, label=None): """Horizontal forest plot of one coefficient vector keyed by level.""" levels = list(post[coord].values) for i, level in enumerate(levels): draws = post.sel({coord: level}).values.ravel() lo, hi = az.hdi(draws, prob=0.94) ax.plot([lo, hi], [i + offset, i + offset], color=colors[level], lw=3) ax.plot( draws.mean(), i + offset, "o", color=colors[level], ms=7, label=label if i == 0 else None, ) if truth is not None: ax.plot( truth[level], i + offset, "x", color="black", ms=9, mew=2, label="true value" if i == 0 and label is None else None, ) ax.set_yticks(range(len(levels))) ax.set_yticklabels(levels) ax.set_ylim(len(levels) - 0.5, -0.5) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIG_WIDTH, FIG_HEIGHT * 0.6)) forest_by_level( ax, idata.posterior["beta_y_region"], "y_region_levels", TRUE_EFFECT, COLORS ) ax.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=1, ls=":") ax.set_xlabel("Effect relative to north (outcome units)") ax.set_ylabel("Level") ax.legend(loc="lower right") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Posterior mean and 94% HDI for each treatment-coded region contrast (relative to north), with the true simulated effect marked as a black × on the region's HDI bar. The wider interval for west reflects its smaller group size (n = 50).](categorical_predictors_files/figure-html/fig-level-effects-recovery-output-1.png){#fig-level-effects-recovery width=664 height=220} ::: ::: **Takeaway:** the posteriors bracket the planted contrasts, and uncertainty scales with group size exactly as it should. The rest of the notebook builds on this validated fit. ## Choosing the reference level with `C()` Automatic inference picks the first level in sorted order (`north`) as the reference. That is often not the comparison you care about. The explicit `C()` syntax makes every coding decision visible in the specification: ``` C(variable, reference=, prior='independent' | 'hierarchical') ``` Here we ask for `south` as the baseline. The design columns change accordingly: ::: {#e4c74d4b .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_south = pathmc.model("y ~ x + C(region, reference='south')", data=df) model_south.design("y").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

0 1.0 -0.941384 0.0 1.0
1 1.0 0.791763 1.0 0.0
2 1.0 -0.505302 1.0 0.0
``` ::: ::: ::: {#01591a74 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} idata_south = model_south.fit(random_seed=42, progressbar=False) az.summary( idata_south, var_names=["beta_y_region"], ci_prob=0.94, ci_kind="hdi", round_to=2, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` NUTS[nutpie]: [beta_y_region, beta_y, sigma_y] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

beta_y_region[west] -3.03 0.09 -3.20 -2.85 2338.47 2556.87 1.0 0.0 0.0

It is important to see that this is a **reparametrization, not a different model**: the fitted values, the residual scale, and any pairwise contrast are the same whichever reference you pick. @fig-reference-reparam demonstrates this by computing the west-minus-north contrast from both fits. Under `reference='north'` it is simply $\beta_{\text{west}}$; under `reference='south'` it is $\beta_{\text{west}} - \beta_{\text{north}}$. ::: {#cell-fig-reference-reparam .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} post_n = idata.posterior["beta_y_region"] post_s = idata_south.posterior["beta_y_region"] west_minus_north_ref_n = post_n.sel(y_region_levels="west").values.ravel() west_minus_north_ref_s = ( post_s.sel(y_region_levels="west") - post_s.sel(y_region_levels="north") ).values.ravel() fig, (ax_l, ax_r) = plt.subplots( 1, 2, figsize=(FIG_WIDTH, FIG_HEIGHT * 0.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1]} ) rows = [ ("south vs north", post_n.sel(y_region_levels="south"), "south", "o"), ("west vs north", post_n.sel(y_region_levels="west"), "west", "o"), ("north vs south", post_s.sel(y_region_levels="north"), "north", "s"), ("west vs south", post_s.sel(y_region_levels="west"), "west", "s"), ] for i, (name, da, level, marker) in enumerate(rows): draws = da.values.ravel() lo, hi = az.hdi(draws, prob=0.94) ax_l.plot([lo, hi], [i, i], color=COLORS[level], lw=3) ax_l.plot(draws.mean(), i, marker, color=COLORS[level], ms=7) ax_l.set_yticks(range(len(rows))) ax_l.set_yticklabels([r[0] for r in rows]) ax_l.invert_yaxis() ax_l.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=1, ls=":") ax_l.set_xlabel("Contrast (outcome units)") ax_l.set_title("Coefficients depend on the reference", fontsize=10) grid = np.linspace(-1.5, -0.5, 300) for draws, ls, label in [ (west_minus_north_ref_n, "-", "from reference = north"), (west_minus_north_ref_s, "--", "from reference = south"), ]: ax_r.plot( grid, gaussian_kde(draws)(grid), color=COLORS["west"], ls=ls, lw=2, label=label ) ax_r.axvline(TRUE_EFFECT["west"], color="black", ls="--", lw=1.5, label="truth") ax_r.set_xlabel("west − north (outcome units)") ax_r.set_ylabel("Posterior density") ax_r.set_title("Contrasts do not", fontsize=10) ax_r.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: posterior contrasts under reference = north (circles) and reference = south (squares); the coefficients differ because they answer different questions. Right: the west − north contrast reconstructed from each fit overlaps almost perfectly with the truth of −1, showing that the reference level is a reparametrization and not a modeling assumption.](categorical_predictors_files/figure-html/fig-reference-reparam-output-1.png){#fig-reference-reparam width=669 height=297} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Which reference should I choose? Pick the level you want the other coefficients to be compared against — usually a control condition, a status-quo policy, or the largest group (which gives the intercept the tightest posterior). If no single baseline is natural, use the intercept-free coding described next and compute contrasts afterwards. ::: ## Cell-means coding with `0 +` Dropping the intercept with `0 +` changes the coding scheme. With no intercept to absorb a baseline, **every** level gets its own indicator column and coefficient, and the column names lose the `T.` marker: ::: {#9a80369f .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_cells = pathmc.model("y ~ 0 + x + region", data=df) model_cells.design("y").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
x region[north] region[south] region[west]
0 -0.941384 0.0 0.0 1.0
1 0.791763 1.0 0.0 0.0
2 -0.505302 1.0 0.0 0.0
``` ::: ::: Each coefficient is now the expected outcome for that level at $x = 0$ — a **cell mean** — rather than a difference from a reference. Since the true group means are 1, 3, and 0, that is what the fit should return (@fig-cell-means). ::: {#1ac0d7c5 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} idata_cells = model_cells.fit(random_seed=42, progressbar=False) az.summary( idata_cells, var_names=["beta_y_region"], ci_prob=0.94, ci_kind="hdi", round_to=2, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` NUTS[nutpie]: [beta_y_region, beta_y, sigma_y] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

Both are full rank; the choice is about which quantities you want the coefficients to represent directly. | Specification | Coefficient vector | Columns | Each coefficient means | |---|---|---|---| | `y ~ region` (intercept present) | one per **non-reference** level | `region[T.south]`, `region[T.west]` | difference from the reference level | | `y ~ 0 + region` (intercept suppressed) | one per **level** | `region[north]`, `region[south]`, `region[west]` | expected outcome for that level | ## Priors on level effects ### Independent priors (default) By default every categorical coefficient gets an independent `Normal(0, 10)` prior — the same weakly informative default as ordinary slopes. You override it by name, exactly like other coefficients. A scalar prior is broadcast across levels: ::: {#d1186b41 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_prior = pathmc.model("y ~ x + region", data=df) model_prior.set_priors({"beta_y_region": Prior("Normal", mu=0, sigma=2)}) model_prior.priors() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=16} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{y,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=2) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: To give **different levels different priors**, pass vectors and name the level dimension. The order follows the coordinate shown by `model.pymc_model.coords`, which is the non-reference levels in their frozen order — here `south` then `west`. The values below are purely illustrative (a mildly informative belief that south is above the reference and west is below it), not the simulated truths: ::: {#2578c0d1 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_prior.set_priors({ "beta_y_region": Prior( "Normal", mu=[1.0, -0.5], sigma=[1.0, 1.0], dims=("y_region_levels",) ) }) model_prior.priors() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=17} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{y,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=[ 1. -0.5],\, sigma=[1. 1.]) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Integer codes sort as strings When levels come from `C()` on an integer column, coordinate order is the *string* sort of the codes: twelve stores coded `1..12` are ordered `1, 10, 11, 12, 2, 3, ...`. Always read the order from `model.pymc_model.coords` before writing a per-level vector prior, or declare the column as a pandas `Categorical` with the order you want. ::: ### Hierarchical shrinkage With a handful of well-populated levels, independent priors are fine. Categorical predictors often have **many** levels with **very unequal** counts — dozens of stores, hundreds of postcodes — and then the sparse levels produce noisy, overconfident-looking estimates. A `prior='hierarchical'` term places a shared population distribution over the level effects: $$ \beta_{\ell} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\beta, \sigma_\beta), \qquad \mu_\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10), \qquad \sigma_\beta \sim \text{HalfNormal}(1) $$ so that levels with little data are pulled towards the population mean by an amount the data itself decides through $\sigma_\beta$. This adds two named hyperparameters, `mu_beta_{outcome}_{variable}` and `sigma_beta_{outcome}_{variable}`: ::: {#11e22761 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} pathmc.model("y ~ x + C(region, prior='hierarchical')", data=df).priors() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=18} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \mu_{beta,y,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{beta,y,region} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{y,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu\_beta\_y\_region,\, sigma\_beta\_y\_region) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: To see the effect, we simulate a second dataset with twelve stores whose sample sizes range from 3 to 80, and compare the independent and hierarchical fits using cell-means coding so every store gets a directly comparable coefficient. ::: {#117c4f87 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} store_rng = np.random.default_rng(7) N_PER_STORE = [3, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80] STORE_IDS = [f"s{i:02d}" for i in range(len(N_PER_STORE))] TRUE_STORE_MEAN = dict(zip(STORE_IDS, 5.0 + store_rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=12))) store = np.repeat(STORE_IDS, N_PER_STORE) stores_df = pd.DataFrame({ "store": store, "y": np.array([TRUE_STORE_MEAN[s] for s in store]) + store_rng.normal(scale=2.0, size=store.size), }) independent = pathmc.model("y ~ 0 + C(store)", data=stores_df) hierarchical = pathmc.model("y ~ 0 + C(store, prior='hierarchical')", data=stores_df) idata_ind = independent.fit(random_seed=7, progressbar=False) idata_hier = hierarchical.fit(random_seed=7, progressbar=False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` NUTS[nutpie]: Stores are ordered by sample size. Bottom: 94% HDI width per store. Hierarchical shrinkage tightens the sparse stores substantially while leaving the well-populated stores almost unchanged.](categorical_predictors_files/figure-html/fig-hierarchical-shrinkage-output-1.png){#fig-hierarchical-shrinkage width=662 height=566} ::: ::: **Takeaway:** for the three stores with only three or four observations, the independent posterior is wide and jumps towards whatever noise those few rows contained, while the hierarchical posterior is pulled towards the population mean and is markedly narrower. From roughly 15 observations upward the two agree, because the data then dominate the prior. This is partial pooling working as intended, and it is why `prior='hierarchical'` is the recommended choice whenever a categorical has many or sparsely observed levels. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Shrinkage is not free Partial pooling trades a little bias for a lot of variance reduction. A genuinely unusual level with very few observations will be pulled towards the crowd. If you have strong prior knowledge that one level is different, encode it through the hyperprior on `sigma_beta_*` (a larger scale permits more spread) or give that level its own independent term. ::: ## Intervening by label Treatment coding is an *internal* representation. When you intervene you speak in **labels**, and pathmc rebuilds the indicator matrix for you: setting the reference selects the all-zero row, setting any other level activates its indicator. The `do()` operator applies this to every row and averages over the remaining covariates, which is g-computation of the interventional mean $E[y \mid do(\text{region} = \ell)]$. ::: {#cb15167c .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} interventions = {level: model.do(set={"region": level}) for level in LEVELS} {level: round(r.mean("y"), 2) for level, r in interventions.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` {'north': 1.02, 'south': 2.98, 'west': -0.04} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-do-by-label .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIG_WIDTH, FIG_HEIGHT * 0.8)) grid = np.linspace(-0.6, 3.6, 500) for level in LEVELS: draws = interventions[level].draws("y") density = gaussian_kde(draws)(grid) ax.fill_between(grid, density, alpha=0.3, color=COLORS[level]) ax.plot(grid, density, color=COLORS[level], lw=2, label=f"do(region = {level})") ax.axvline(TRUE_GROUP_MEAN[level], color=COLORS[level], ls="--", lw=1.5) ax.set_xlabel("E[y | do(region = level)] (outcome units)") ax.set_ylabel("Posterior density") ax.legend(loc="upper center") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Posterior distribution of the interventional mean E[y | do(region = level)] for each region, obtained by setting every store to that level and averaging over x. The `ate()` wrapper does the same in one call and returns an `EstimandResult` that knows its outcome: ::: {#167f79b0 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} contrast = interventions["south"] - interventions["north"] print( f"E[y | do(south)] − E[y | do(north)] = {contrast.mean('y'):.2f}, " f"94% HDI {np.round(contrast.hdi('y'), 2)}" ) model.ate("y", "region", values=("north", "south")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` E[y | do(south)] − E[y | do(north)] = 1.96, 94% HDI [1.84 2.09] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Mixing categorical and continuous interventions A single `do()` call can set a categorical label alongside a numeric value. Four query methods accept labels today — `do()`, `ate()`, `prob()`, and `cate()` — as interventions (`set=`, `values=`) and as conditions (`condition=`); the remaining helpers are listed under the boundaries at the end of this page: ::: {#9522e0fb .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} both = model.do(set={"region": "west", "x": 1.0}) print( f"E[y | do(region = west, x = 1)] = {both.mean('y'):.2f} " f"(truth {TRUE_INTERCEPT + TRUE_SLOPE_X * 1.0 + TRUE_EFFECT['west']:.2f})" ) print( f"P(y > 2 | do(region = south)) = {model.prob('y > 2', set={'region': 'south'}):.2f}" ) model.cate("y", "x", values=(0.0, 1.0), condition={"region": "south"}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` E[y | do(region = west, x = 1)] = 0.45 (truth 0.50) P(y > 2 | do(region = south)) = 0.91 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `kind="predictive"` propagates the residual noise as well, giving the posterior predictive distribution of an individual store's outcome under the intervention rather than the interventional mean: ::: {#d18a1758 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} predictive = model.do(set={"region": "south"}, kind="predictive") print( f"mean {predictive.mean('y'):.2f}, 94% interval {np.round(predictive.hdi('y'), 2)}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean 2.98, 94% interval [1.58 4.35] ``` ::: ::: The predictive interval is far wider than the interval on the mean in @fig-do-by-label because it includes the $\sigma_y = 0.5$ observation noise. ## Predicting for new rows `predict(data=...)` runs posterior predictive sampling with replacement predictor values. Categorical columns in the new frame are encoded with the **fitted** level set and reference, so it does not matter whether the levels arrive in a different row order or whether a level happens to be absent from the new frame. Here we move every store one region along a fixed cycle, so every row's region changes: ::: {#f5b274d4 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} NEXT_REGION = {"north": "south", "south": "west", "west": "north"} new_rows = df.assign(region=df["region"].map(NEXT_REGION)) pp = model.predict(data=new_rows, extend_inferencedata=False, progressbar=False) predicted_mean = pp.posterior_predictive["y"].mean(("chain", "draw")).values pd.DataFrame({ "region": new_rows["region"], "x": new_rows["x"].round(2), "predicted mean": predicted_mean.round(2), "true mean": ( TRUE_INTERCEPT + TRUE_SLOPE_X * new_rows["x"] + new_rows["region"].map(TRUE_EFFECT) ).round(2), }).head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The replacement frame must have the same number of rows as the fitted data (variable-length posterior prediction is not supported yet), and it must contain every predictor column the model uses. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## If you see `RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in divide` Running these `predict()` and `do()` cells locally may print a NumPy `RuntimeWarning` from inside PyTensor. When PyMC checks whether the indicator matrix changed, PyTensor computes a relative error $|a-b|/(|a|+|b|)$ for a log message, which is $0/0$ wherever both the old and new indicator entries are zero. The warning is cosmetic: the comparison result is correct and the samples are unaffected. The rendered page hides it with `warning: false`. ::: ### Unseen levels raise, never guess If a level appears at prediction or intervention time that was not observed during fitting, pathmc raises a `ValueError` that names the predictor, the offending level, and the levels it knows about. This is deliberate: the alternative — silently rebuilding the contrast matrix from the new data, as `pandas.get_dummies` or a fresh `patsy` call would — changes what every coefficient means without telling you. ::: {#54467666 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} for attempt in ( lambda: model.predict(data=df.assign(region="central"), extend_inferencedata=False), lambda: model.do(set={"region": "central"}), ): try: attempt() except ValueError as err: print(f"ValueError: {err}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ValueError: Categorical predictor 'region' contains unseen level(s) ['central']. Fitted levels are ['north', 'south', 'west']. ValueError: Categorical predictor 'region' contains unseen level(s) ['central']. Fitted levels are ['north', 'south', 'west']. ``` ::: ::: ## The frozen level set The prediction and intervention behaviours above all follow from one design decision, sketched in @fig-frozen-state: the level set is resolved exactly once, at `model()` time, and every later call only swaps rows into the compiled indicator matrix. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-frozen-state %%| fig-cap: "Lifecycle of a categorical predictor. Level set, reference, and column names are resolved once from the fitting data and stored on the model. Prediction and intervention re-encode labels against that frozen state; anything outside it is rejected rather than re-inferred." flowchart LR D["fitting data
region: strings"] --> F["resolve once
levels = [north, south, west]
reference = north
columns = region[T.south], region[T.west]"] F --> C["compile
pm.Data indicator matrix
beta_y_region[y_region_levels]"] C --> P["predict(data=new)
re-encode labels → swap matrix"] C --> I["do(set={region: label})
encode one label for all rows → swap matrix"] F -. "unseen label" .-> E["ValueError naming
predictor, level, fitted levels"] P -.-> E I -.-> E ``` ### Controlling the reference without `C()` The "resolve once" step reads a pandas `Categorical` column's **declared category order**, so making the desired baseline the first category is an alternative to `reference=`. Declaring `["west", "south", "north"]` should make `west` the reference and leave indicator columns for `south` and `north`, in that order: ::: {#05862460 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} ordered = df.assign( region=pd.Categorical(df["region"], categories=["west", "south", "north"]) ) pathmc.model("y ~ x + region", data=ordered).design("y").columns.tolist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ``` ['Intercept', 'x', 'region[T.south]', 'region[T.north]'] ``` ::: ::: Categories that are declared but never observed are dropped from the level set (they cannot be estimated), and using one later triggers the unseen-level error. ## Numeric codes as categories Integer-coded groups are common — `store_type` as 1, 2, 3 — and they are ambiguous: the numbers could be magnitudes or arbitrary labels. pathmc keeps integers **continuous by default** and lets `C()` declare that they are labels. When it does, the labels are also excluded from any [scaling](/user-guide/categorical-predictors.html#scaling-and-numeric-labels) you apply to channels: dividing a group code by its maximum would be meaningless. ::: {#19ebb110 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} coded = df.assign(store_type=rng.choice([1, 2, 3], size=len(df))) as_number = pathmc.model("y ~ x + store_type", data=coded) as_label = pathmc.model( "y ~ x + C(store_type)", data=coded, scaling=pathmc.Scaling(channel={"method": "max"}), ) print("continuous:", as_number.design("y").columns.tolist()) print("categorical:", as_label.design("y").columns.tolist()) print("scaled columns:", as_label.fitted_scaling.columns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` continuous: ['Intercept', 'x', 'store_type'] categorical: ['Intercept', 'x', 'store_type[T.2]', 'store_type[T.3]'] scaled columns: ('x',) ``` ::: ::: Only `x` received a scale factor; the `store_type` labels were left untouched. ## Categoricals in multi-equation models A categorical predictor can appear in several structural equations. Each equation gets its own coefficient vector — `beta_m_region` and `beta_y_region` below — and `do()` propagates a label change through the whole graph. Here the region affects the outcome both directly and through a mediator `m`: ::: {#ae2a6511 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} med_rng = np.random.default_rng(5) m = 0.5 + 1.0 * (df["region"] == "south") + med_rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=len(df)) y_med = ( 1.0 + 0.8 * m + df["region"].map(TRUE_EFFECT) + med_rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=len(df)) ) med_df = pd.DataFrame({"region": df["region"], "m": m, "y": y_med}) mediation = pathmc.model( """ m ~ region y ~ m + region """, data=med_df, ) mediation.equations() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=31} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{m} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{m} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{m,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{y,region} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\[6pt] \mu_{m} &= \beta_{0,\,m} + \operatorname{C}(\mathrm{region};\,\mathrm{ref}=north;\,\mathrm{levels}=\{north, south, west\}) \\ \mathrm{m} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{m},\, \sigma_{m}) \\ \mu_{y} &= \beta_{0,\,y} + \mathrm{m} + \operatorname{C}(\mathrm{region};\,\mathrm{ref}=north;\,\mathrm{levels}=\{north, south, west\}) \\ \mathrm{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{y},\, \sigma_{y}) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: ::: {#6bfaa38a .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} mediation.fit(random_seed=5, progressbar=False) total = mediation.do(set={"region": "south"}) - mediation.do(set={"region": "north"}) print( f"Total effect of south vs north on y: {total.mean('y'):.2f}, " f"94% HDI {np.round(total.hdi('y'), 2)} " f"(truth = direct 2.0 + indirect 0.8 × 1.0 = 2.8)" ) print( f"Effect on the mediator m: {total.mean('m'):.2f}, " f"94% HDI {np.round(total.hdi('m'), 2)} (truth 1.0)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Total effect of south vs north on y: 2.75, 94% HDI [2.61 2.88] (truth = direct 2.0 + indirect 0.8 × 1.0 = 2.8) Effect on the mediator m: 0.94, 94% HDI [0.87 1.01] (truth 1.0) ``` ::: ::: The `DoResult` describes the whole system, so the same contrast object reports the effect on `m` and on `y`. ## Simulating from a model with categoricals `pathmc.simulate()` accepts the same specification and draws outcomes from fixed parameter values. The categorical coefficient vector is supplied under its usual name with one entry per represented level, in the frozen level order; `simulate_params_template()` reports the shapes you need: ::: {#02f23f6d .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} exog = df[["x", "region"]] pathmc.simulate_params_template("y ~ x + region", data=exog) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33} ``` {'beta_y_region': {'kind': 'vector', 'shape': (2,), 'dtype': 'float64'}, 'beta_y': {'kind': 'vector', 'shape': (2,), 'dtype': 'float64'}, 'sigma_y': {'kind': 'scalar', 'shape': (), 'dtype': 'float64'}} ``` ::: ::: ::: {#2d2034cb .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} simulated = pathmc.simulate( "y ~ x + region", data=exog, params={ "beta_y": [TRUE_INTERCEPT, TRUE_SLOPE_X], "beta_y_region": [TRUE_EFFECT["south"], TRUE_EFFECT["west"]], "sigma_y": 0.5, }, random_seed=0, ) simulated.groupby("region", observed=True)["y"].mean().round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34} ``` region north 1.03 south 3.12 west -0.08 Name: y, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ## Capability reference The full surface in one place. Rows marked † were not exercised above; they follow the same rules and are covered in the [user guide](/user-guide/categorical-predictors.html). | Capability | How | Notes | |---|---|---| | Automatic detection | `y ~ region` | string / `Categorical` / `StringDtype` / string-valued `object` columns | | Explicit declaration | `y ~ C(region)` | required for integer-coded labels | | Choose the reference | `C(region, reference='south')` | reference must be an observed level | | Cell-means coding | `y ~ 0 + region` | one coefficient per level, columns `region[level]` | | Independent priors | default; override `beta_{lhs}_{var}` | scalar broadcasts; vectors need `dims=("{lhs}_{var}_levels",)` | | Hierarchical priors | `C(region, prior='hierarchical')` | adds `mu_beta_{lhs}_{var}` and `sigma_beta_{lhs}_{var}` | | Introspection | `equations()`, `design()`, `priors()`, `graph()`† | posteriors indexed by level name | | Intervene by label | `do(set={"region": "south"})` | mixes freely with numeric `set=` values; `kind="predictive"` supported | | Causal contrasts | `ate(outcome, "region", values=(a, b))`, `DoResult` subtraction | any pair of observed labels | | Probability & subgroup queries | `prob(expr, set={...})`, `cate(..., condition={"region": ...})` | labels accepted as interventions and conditions | | Predict on new rows | `predict(data=new_df)` | same row count; frozen encoding; unseen levels raise | | Simulation | `simulate(..., params={"beta_{lhs}_{var}": [...]})` | one entry per represented level | | Multiple equations | `m ~ region; y ~ m + region` | one coefficient vector per equation | | Non-Gaussian outcomes† | `families={"y": "bernoulli"}` etc. | coding is independent of the likelihood | | Scaling | `scaling=Scaling(channel=...)` | numeric labels excluded from channel scaling | | Polars and other frames† | pass any narwhals-compatible frame | inspected via pandas | The boundaries most likely to matter in practice are below; the complete error contract, with every message and its workaround, lives in the user guide's [errors table](/user-guide/categorical-predictors.html#errors-you-may-see). | Not supported today | What happens | Workaround | |---|---|---| | Interactions involving a categorical (`region:x`) | `NotImplementedError` at build | fit separate models per level, or build indicator × x columns by hand | | Categorical outcomes (`region ~ x`) | `NotImplementedError` at build | recode to a numeric or 0/1 outcome and choose a suitable family | | Panel models with a categorical | `NotImplementedError` at build | fit cross-sectionally, or encode indicators manually | | Unseen levels in `predict()` / `do()` | `ValueError` naming the level | only fitted levels can be predicted or intervened on | | Labels in `predictions()` / `comparisons()` / `slopes()` / `att()` / `atu()` / `effect()` | not yet routed | use `do()`, `ate()`, `prob()`, and `cate()` as shown above | ## Summary - String and categorical columns are detected automatically and **treatment coded**; wrap integer codes in `C()` to declare them as labels. - With an intercept, one level is the **reference** (first sorted level, first declared category, or `reference=`) and every other level gets a named coefficient in `beta_{lhs}_{var}`, indexed by level name. With `0 +`, every level gets a coefficient. - The reference is a **reparametrization**: pairwise contrasts are identical whichever level you choose. - `prior='hierarchical'` partially pools level effects and is the right default for many or sparsely observed levels. - The level set is **frozen at build time**. `do()` and `predict()` re-encode labels against it; unseen levels raise instead of silently changing the coding. - Interventions and contrasts are expressed in **labels** — `do(set={"region": "south"})`, `ate("y", "region", values=("north", "south"))` — and compose with numeric interventions. ### Next steps - [The do() Operator](causal_do_operator.qmd) — the full intervention API these label-based calls build on. - [Custom Priors](custom_priors.qmd) — more on overriding and checking priors, including prior predictive checks. - [Categorical Predictors (user guide)](/user-guide/categorical-predictors.html) — the reference for inference rules, coding schemes, parameter names, priors, and the error contract. - [Model Specification](/user-guide/model-specification.html) — the full DSL reference.
